before.claim: RNA polymerase binds a DNA region and uses one DNA strand as the template to synthesize an RNA strand. Transcription copies a selected DNA region into one RNA transcript. RNA polymerase reads a DNA template and creates phosphodiester links in the nascent RNA; after it passes, the local DNA duplex reforms. This is not a second round of DNA replication.

RNA transcription copies a selected region rather than producing a second chromosome, so a cell can transcribe a gene repeatedly between divisions. before.claim: During RNA synthesis, DNA A pairs with RNA U, DNA T pairs with RNA A, and DNA C and G pair with RNA G and C respectively. Hydrogen bonding supports the matching of a ribonucleotide to its template base while RNA polymerase creates the covalent sugar–phosphate backbone of the new RNA.

The RNA sequence is complementary and antiparallel to the template DNA strand. It matches the coding DNA strand apart from U in RNA in place of T in DNA, provided both sequences are written 5′ to 3′. Confusing these two DNA strands reverses expected RNA and codon answers.

Check the polarity of all three aligned molecules: coding DNA 5′-ATG GCT TAA-3′, template DNA 3′-TAC CGA ATT-5′, and mRNA 5′-AUG GCU UAA-3′. RNA is complementary to the template and matches the coding sequence apart from U replacing T.

If the DNA template reads 3′-TAC CGA ATT-5′, the RNA transcript reads 5′-AUG GCU UAA-3′. The corresponding coding DNA strand is 5′-ATG GCT TAA-3′, which matches the RNA apart from thymine being replaced by uracil. Hydrogen bonding selects each matching ribonucleotide, but covalent phosphodiester bonds join the RNA strand. A question that merely gives a DNA sequence without indicating template versus coding strand and direction cannot have one uniquely specified RNA answer.

before.claim: A DNA gene can be transcribed repeatedly because RNA polymerase reads the sequence without consuming nucleotides from the DNA template or converting DNA into RNA. The double helix re-forms when the temporary transcription bubble passes, preserving the base order.

A neuron may remain active for years with little or no cell division while making fresh RNA copies from the same DNA genes. Maintenance and DNA repair matter because a persistent template mutation could alter all later transcripts produced from that gene.

A differentiated neuron may need the same protein for years without duplicating its entire genome. RNA polymerase temporarily separates a short stretch of DNA, constructs an RNA transcript, and leaves the DNA bases in their original order; the DNA duplex can re-form immediately behind it. Multiple transcripts can be synthesized from a gene at different times. Replication, by contrast, produces another DNA molecule before division. This difference explains why ongoing gene expression is compatible with maintaining a stable inherited DNA sequence in cells that rarely divide.

after.claim: RNA polymerase reads the DNA base sequence without consuming it or turning it into RNA. The locally separated strands rejoin after transcription, leaving the original sequence available to be read again.

before.claim: Most cells share a large collection of genes, but they do not transcribe every gene at the same time. Transcription is an early control point for gene expression: if a gene is not transcribed, little or no new mRNA from it becomes available for translation.

A liver cell and a pancreatic beta cell can carry the same insulin gene while producing different quantities of its transcript. Regulatory proteins and DNA regions are further explored in HL gene expression, but the essential idea is selective transcription rather than a change to DNA sequence.

Not every gene is transcribed continuously. Regulatory choices at transcription help cells with essentially the same genome maintain different patterns of protein synthesis and different specialized functions. Gene expression describes molecular activity, not a change in the DNA genotype.

A cell may contain a gene in its genome while producing little or none of that gene's RNA. Regulatory signals can change transcription initiation at its promoter, changing the number of transcripts available for translation. Different amounts of a polypeptide can change metabolic activity or cellular structure and thus alter phenotype. This helps explain why cells derived from one zygote develop different functions despite inheriting very similar DNA sequences. Presence of a gene therefore does not imply that it is continuously expressed in every cell type.

after.claim: Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time. Transcription is the first stage of gene expression and a key point at which a gene can be switched on or off. If a protein-coding gene is not transcribed, no new mRNA from it is supplied for translation.

Cells with essentially the same genes can produce different proteins because they transcribe different genes. For example, pancreatic beta cells transcribe the insulin gene much more actively than most other cells. This changes cell function without requiring a change in the gene’s DNA sequence.

before.claim: Translation converts the sequence of mRNA codons into an amino-acid sequence, rather than copying a nucleic acid strand. Ribosomes assemble amino acids through peptide bonds in the order specified by the mRNA. A resulting polypeptide may fold and undergo additional processing before functioning as a protein.

The codon AUG at the beginning of a coding sequence specifies methionine and usually signals translation initiation. Stop codons terminate the coded chain instead of specifying an extra amino acid. The final polypeptide is read from the amino terminus toward the carboxyl terminus.

before.claim: The ribosome reads the next mRNA codon in the 5′→3′ direction. A tRNA carrying an amino acid enters the A (aminoacyl) site when its anticodon can pair with that codon. The P (peptidyl) site already holds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide. The tRNA is an adaptor: its anticodon matches the instruction, while its attached amino acid supplies the material.

The ribosome catalyses a peptide bond between the growing chain and the amino acid on the A-site tRNA. The chain transfers from the P-site tRNA to the A-site tRNA and becomes one amino acid longer at its carboxyl end. The mRNA itself does not become part of the polypeptide; it determines the order in which amino acids are added.

The ribosome then translocates by one codon—three mRNA bases—towards the 3′ end. The tRNA now bearing the growing chain shifts into the P site, and the empty tRNA moves towards the E (exit) site and leaves. The A site becomes available for the next matching aminoacyl-tRNA. This repeating sequence explains why the reading frame must be maintained; moving one or two bases would change subsequent codons.

after.claim: During elongation, a tRNA with a complementary anticodon brings the amino acid specified by the next mRNA codon. The ribosome forms a peptide bond, transferring the growing chain from its tRNA to the incoming amino acid.

The ribosome moves along mRNA by one codon, or three bases. The empty tRNA leaves, and the tRNA carrying the chain remains positioned for the next cycle. Repeating selection, peptide-bond formation and movement builds the polypeptide in codon order. The A, P and E site names shown in the detailed figure are developed in D1.2.17 (HL); the shared requirement here is the elongation sequence.

before.claim: A DNA point mutation may change an mRNA codon and thus replace an amino acid. The biochemical properties of the replacement can affect folding, stability or activity, but not every substitution produces a change in the encoded polypeptide.

In sickle-cell disease, a substitution in the beta-globin gene can replace glutamate with valine in beta-globin, affecting hemoglobin properties. The example shows that a molecular sequence difference can have consequences at cell and organism levels, not that all variants cause disease.

A point substitution can alter one codon and thereby change one amino acid. Altered side-chain chemistry may affect folding, binding or an active site; the effect depends on protein context. The sickle-cell HBB substitution is one example, but a substitution is not always harmful.

A DNA base substitution can result in a changed mRNA codon and a different amino acid in the translated chain. Depending on its location and properties, that replacement may alter protein folding or function, but some substitutions are synonymous and do not change the amino-acid sequence. A premature stop signal can shorten the product and often has more severe effects. Work through the DNA-to-mRNA-to-polypeptide sequence before predicting phenotype. Not every DNA mutation affects a protein, and even a changed amino acid is not necessarily biologically damaging.
